name: Ethereum Classic
classificationNote: Upstream label "Bridge & Cross-Chain / Forged Proof" on a base-layer chain: reclassified as a 51%/consensus attack.
rootCause: Bitfly officially tweeted that ETC encountered another large-scale 51% attack today. The attack has resulted in the reorganization of more than 4000 blocks. Bitfly reminded that unless the official notified further, the current mining pool payment is invalid. At the same time, the government encourages all miners to switch ETH pools on the official website. Blockchain data analysis company Bitquery released an investigation report on the second 51% attack of ETC. The report shows that the initiator of this attack and the initiator of the first attack were the same miner. The attackers profited at least 1.68 million US dollars from this attack.

descriptions.text: Bitfly officially tweeted that ETC encountered another large-scale 51% attack today. The attack has resulted in the reorganization of more than 4000 blocks. Bitfly reminded that unless the official notified further, the current mining pool payment is invalid. At the same time, the government encourages all miners to switch ETH pools on the official website. Blockchain data analysis company Bitquery released an investigation report on the second 51% attack of ETC. The report shows that the initiator of this attack and the initiator of the first attack were the same miner. The attackers profited at least 1.68 million US dollars from this attack.

Bitfly tweeted that today, the ETC blockchain has undergone a chain reorganization of 3693 blocks at a block height of 10904146. This causes all state construction nodes to stop synchronizing. The ETC blockchain did not produce blocks for nearly 6 hours, and then the block production returned to normal.

On August 6, 2020, Ethereum Classic suffered a second major 51% attack that resulted in a reorganization of 4,236 blocks and an estimated loss of $1.68 million (238,306 ETC) through successful double-spends. This exploit was enabled by rented hashpower, not a contract vulnerability. The attacker controlled a majority of network hashpower and reorganized the chain to double-spend funds, exploiting Ethereum Classic's low Proof-of-Work security and absence of external checkpointing. No smart contract was directly vulnerable.
